kicker: Cobalt Analytix · Prepared for PlayBlue · Executive Summary
title: PlayBlue: what the _evidence_ says before the doors open
lede: A sector and client analysis assembled from public sources ahead of our working session, with every figure verified against primary filings where possible and every disagreement between sources shown rather than resolved silently. It sizes the opportunity from first principles, tests PlayBlue's plan against what Indian multi-brand sports retail has actually done, and names the decisions still open ahead of the Bengaluru launch. This page distills the six findings that matter most — the full evidence, market data, competitive arena, and proposal live on the [detailed research](/detailed-research) page.

findings.title: The plan implies roughly triple Decathlon's sales density, on a third of the gross margin
findings.desc: The arithmetic a diligent investor runs first, run here: revenue per store, per square foot, against the category leader.

body.label: A second test, at store level
body.text: A 15,000 sq ft Bengaluru high-street flagship (Indiranagar 100 Feet Road, ₹200/sq ft/month asking) carries roughly ₹6.3 Cr/yr in rent, CAM, staffing for the expert-guidance model, and overhead. At 30% gross margin, that store needs ₹21.1 Cr in revenue — ₹14,100/sq ft/yr — just to cover its own fixed costs, before warehouse, e-commerce build, corporate overhead or markdown. That figure is already above Decathlon's demonstrated density.

body.label: Why this matters commercially
body.text: This doesn't say the plan is unachievable. It says it requires a sales density no Indian sports retailer has demonstrated, and that the case for it needs to be made explicitly rather than assumed. A Series A conversation opens here.

findings.title: Layer 3 has been occupied before. It has not yet produced a profitable national chain
findings.desc: Multi-brand curated sports retail is not an empty layer in India — it has been attempted repeatedly, at scale, and has not yet worked at national scale.

rows.text: ~₹172 Cr, 70+ stores, 50 cities — Nike, Puma, Adidas, Skechers, Asics, Reebok + own label
Metro Brands (offline) + Nykaa Fashion (online), from Oct 2024

body.label: What follows
body.text: Sports Station has run multi-brand sports retail for years and sits at ~₹172 Cr — roughly 4% of Decathlon. That is the demonstrated ceiling for this model in India so far, and PlayBlue's Phase-1 target is 58% of it in year one. And the most experienced new entrant — Metro Brands, with the capital and the Foot Locker licence to open at any scale — chose 3,333 sq ft in Bengaluru. PlayBlue is planning 15,000 sq ft in the same city.

body.label: Why this matters commercially
body.text: The correct read is not 'the layer is empty.' It is: the layer has been occupied repeatedly and has not yet produced a profitable national chain — and the best-capitalised recent entrant chose a fifth of PlayBlue's planned format size. That format divergence deserves a direct, explicit answer.

findings.title: Gross margin is set by the brands, not by the retailer
findings.desc: Realised multi-brand gross margin runs ~27–32% globally, and the major brands have spent five years reducing how many partners they sell that margin to.

body.label: The evidence
body.text: Nike's Consumer Direct Acceleration strategy cut roughly half its global wholesale accounts to ~40 strategic partners. In India, Nike went from ~80–90 franchisees and ~25 distributors to a handful — closing ~200 of ~350 stores — now working through RiseIndia (~37–43 premium stores since 2022), with SSIPL moved to equipment distribution and Nykaa taking online from Feb 2026. Adidas runs subsidiary plus exclusive-brand franchise, ~750 stores including Reebok, which is now licensed to ABFRL. Puma is a wholly-owned subsidiary, 440+ stores, ~43% of sales online.

body.label: The partial counter-current
body.text: Nike's own leadership has acknowledged over-rotating away from wholesale; Nike wholesale grew 8% to $7.5bn in Q2 FY26 against DTC down 8%. The door is opening slightly. It is not open.

body.label: The test that settles it
body.text: Written allocation terms from the top three brands — MOQ, credit days, season allocation, markdown support, exclusivity — before the 15,000 sq ft lease is signed. Without fresh-season product committed in writing, the store opens with the wrong inventory. That is precisely what happened to Foot Locker when Nike shifted to DTC: ~60% of mix in one brand, structural decline, and a $2.4bn sale to Dick's Sporting Goods in September 2025.

findings.title: Pure curation does not exist at scale anywhere — every survivor runs an owned or exclusive line
findings.desc: The most useful international read, and it reframes the model rather than challenging it.

body.label: The evidence
body.text: JD Sports — the multi-brand survivor — runs ~47% gross margin with own-brand at ~15% of apparel sales and 'Only at JD' exclusives at ~20% of stock units, actively diversifying into challenger brands to cut legacy-brand dependence from ~70%. Metro Brands, the closest Indian equivalent, runs ~50% gross / ~30% EBITDA margin built on owned and exclusive distribution (Clarks, Crocs, Fila, now Foot Locker) — not open-market curation. Foot Locker, without either, ran ~27.5% gross margin, over-depended on one brand's open-market allocation, and was acquired after ~400 planned store closures. Decathlon itself is petitioning to carry other brands, capped at 20% of inventory.

body.label: Why this matters commercially
body.text: The convergent answer across every profitable operator is a mix — roughly 70–80% curated third-party, 20–30% owned or exclusive. This is constructive, not fatal: it argues PlayBlue should plan an owned or exclusive-brand line from day one, potentially via exclusive India distribution for challenger brands (On, Hoka, emerging Indian labels), rather than as a later phase. That is a buying decision being made now, and expensive to reverse once the assortment is set.

findings.title: The addressable base is narrower and richer than the headline projection
findings.desc: The government's own data and the industry's own data both undercut the top-down $30bn figure — while pointing straight at the segment PlayBlue is already targeting.

body.label: What the government measures
body.text: MoSPI's 2024 Time Use Survey: 9.7% of Indians exercised on the reference day (14.5% men, 4.9% women), up from 5.7% in 2019. Sport specifically is under 1%, and over four in five participants are under 20.

body.label: What the industry measures
body.text: Deloitte x HFA: 12.3 million gym members across 46,500 facilities — 0.8% penetration — projected to 23.3 million by 2030. Commercial fitness revenue ₹16,200 Cr (2024) to ₹37,700 Cr (2030). Only ~15% of physically active 18–62-year-olds pay for fitness at all. Exercise participation runs 17% in households above ₹24,000/month against 8.4% below ₹6,500; Karnataka sits at 13.7% against the 9.7% national average.

body.label: Why this matters commercially
body.text: This argues for the strategy, not against it. The commercially relevant base is not 1.4 billion people discovering sport — it is ~12.3 million paying fitness consumers plus affluent urban households exercising at 17%, smaller, wealthier, metro-concentrated, and growing. That profile favours a premium curated format and validates Bengaluru-first. It does not support a top-down market-size claim; the Series A deck should be built bottom-up, from households above an income threshold, within a drive-time, at measured activity rates.

findings.title: Multi-brand retail FDI is a live regulatory question, not a historical footnote
findings.desc: India restricts multi-brand retail FDI while permitting 100% FDI in single-brand retail. This is a question for counsel, not for us — but it is structural to PlayBlue's model.

body.label: The evidence
body.text: India permits 100% FDI in single-brand retail via the automatic route. Multi-brand retail trading requires government approval, is capped at 51%, and carries a $100M minimum inflow, 30% MSME sourcing, and city/state consent conditions. Inventory-model multi-brand e-commerce with foreign capital is restricted; only the marketplace model takes 100% FDI. Decathlon's global CEO has confirmed seeking permission to carry other brands, capped at 20% of inventory — confirming the distinction is actively enforced today.

body.label: Why it is relevant to PlayBlue specifically
body.text: PlayBlue is Indian-founded with minority foreign seed capital (MIXI Global Investments co-leading), so this is not a present-tense problem — it becomes one at the next foreign round if the inventory-holding entity scales, since PlayBlue's core model of reselling 100+ third-party brands is definitionally multi-brand retail trading.

body.label: Why this matters commercially
body.text: This is a structuring question for legal counsel, not a conclusion we are positioned to draw. But given how fundamental it is to a model built entirely on multi-brand curation, it merits a direct conversation before Mumbai and Delhi NCR add further scale — that is the lower-cost point to resolve it.

proposalCallout: A four-week Launch Readiness Diagnostic, run as two parallel tracks: a supply-side track that tests whether the top 100+ brands will allocate fresh-season stock on workable terms, and a demand-side track that tests PlayBlue's four stated differentiators and maps the price corridor against Decathlon — in the last window where the answers can still change the store.
